- Model consistently underestimates prices in early forecast periods (especially first 5–10 days), suggesting a lag or delayed response to recent price trends.
- Overshoots occur after sharp price spikes in history (e.g., 86+ → forecast jumps to 86.48+), indicating overreaction to recent volatility.
- Forecasts tend to be too optimistic in the short term (first 10–15 days) and then gradually converge toward true values — suggesting mean reversion bias in the model.
- Model exhibits persistent downward bias in the latter half of the forecast horizon (last 10–15 days), possibly due to underweighting of recent low prices or overconfidence in prior trends.
- Forecasts often fail to capture the “rebound” after a sharp drop — e.g., after 75–78, model stays low while true price rebounds to 79–82.
- Model overestimates the “recovery” phase after a dip — e.g., after 75–77, forecast jumps to 80+ while true price only reaches 78–80.
- Model underestimates the impact of recent high prices — e.g., when history includes 85–86, forecast often settles at 84–85, missing the “high-pressure” effect.
- Model shows strong bias toward smoothing out volatility — underestimates spikes and overestimates dips, leading to “flat” forecasts in volatile periods.
- Forecasts are often too conservative in the first 5–7 days, then become more aggressive — suggesting a “learning curve” or adaptive bias.
- Model fails to account for “reversal” patterns — e.g., after a 10–15 day downtrend, forecast doesn’t anticipate a rebound, leading to persistent underestimation.
